accuracy.reason: The limits match the sources. An HTTP 202 and a RabbitMQ publisher confirm accept work without completing it. A consumer acknowledgement only retires a delivery. A database transaction with a stable operation ID makes that database effect duplicate-safe and does not create exactly-once delivery. Retries are for transient faults, with a finite budget. A queue that stays behind grows. Kafka offsets record progress under a retention policy and do not by themselves make an external effect exactly once.

evidence.quote: A publisher confirmation means broker acceptance under the configured durability rules, not a completed receipt.
That transaction protects its database effects. It does not make an external email or payment atomic, or turn delivery into a universal exactly-once guarantee.

sourceChecks.claim: A long operation can return HTTP 202 Accepted with a status URL, and that response is not the finished resource. The status resource later reports states such as pending or failed, and a failure has to be stored where the client can read it. Microsoft describes 202 as acknowledgement that the request was accepted for processing, status values including Pending and Failed, and a completed status or redirect only when the work is done.

A publisher confirm covers broker acceptance, including disk persistence for a persistent message on a durable queue and quorum acceptance for a quorum queue, and it does not mean a consumer finished the business work. A consumer acknowledgement tells the broker that delivery can be discarded. RabbitMQ states that publisher confirms are not aware of consumers and that consumer acknowledgements are not aware of publishers, so neither acknowledgement is atomic with a separate database write.

Retries need a stable caller-supplied operation ID, and recording that ID must be atomic with the mutation so a repeat has no extra side effect. AWS requires the idempotency token and the mutating work to commit together, all or nothing, and treats a repeated client token as the same operation. That design bounds the business effect. It does not promise that the message transport delivers exactly once, and it does not make a separate external system atomic with the database transaction.

Retry a transient outage after a delay, increase the delay, and stop after a finite number of attempts. Do not keep retrying a fault that will not succeed, such as a bad input. The retry pattern says commonplace busy faults should be retried with increasing delays up to a maximum, that immediate aggressive retries can deepen an overload, and that a non-transient fault should be canceled and reported. Isolating that reported failure for investigation matches the pattern's cancel-and-report outcome. The page does not say that storing the failure repairs it.

Concurrent consumers can finish dependent messages out of the order they were received, so delivery order is not ordered effects. The competing-consumers page says receive order is not the creation order, that each message goes to one consumer, and that work which must run in sequence is a poor fit unless the same consumer handles the group in sequence, as with sessions. Holding later work for one entity while that entity's earlier work finishes is that sequencing rule, and a single busy entity then limits throughput. A dead-letter destination is for analysis after repeated failure, not for resolving a later message that still depends on the failed one.

A queue absorbs a burst only while later capacity can catch up. If arrivals stay above completions, depth and latency grow, storage and retention are finite, and the producer has to shed or throttle work. Adding consumers without a bound on downstream concurrency moves the overload onto the saturated dependency and increases contention. The load-leveling page states each of those limits and says to monitor queue depth, scale only within safe limits, or shed work at the producer.

A topic is split into ordered partitions. Each consumer group reads independently, one consumer in the group owns a partition at a time, and the group records an offset that does not delete the log. Replay is possible only while retention still holds the records. Kafka says partitions are totally ordered, that each partition is consumed by one member of each group, that consumers can rewind an offset, and that messages are retained for a configured time or size instead of being deleted on consumption. It also says exactly-once handling of an external system needs that system's cooperation, so offsets and retained history alone do not make an external effect exactly once. Order is inside a partition, not across the topic.

Defer work only when the caller can proceed with a job ID and a later status. A decision that the next step needs, such as authorization before showing a private resource, stays on the request. Report ready only after the result exists, and keep a terminal failure visible. Microsoft uses 202 plus a status resource for long work, lists Failed as a terminal status, and recommends a synchronous response when the operation can finish on the same connection. The page also treats the status store and the polling path as extra machinery the client and the service have to operate.
